title: At the Threshing Floor: Ruth Asks Boaz to Redeem
summary: Naomi devises a bold plan to secure a home for Ruth: she is to go at night to the threshing floor where Boaz is sleeping and ask him, in effect, to marry her. Ruth goes, uncovers his feet, and asks him to spread his garment over her as a kinsman-redeemer. Boaz praises her loyalty, promises to act, but reveals that a nearer relative has the first right, and sends her home at dawn with a generous gift of barley.
story: At the end of chapter 2 the barley and wheat harvests are over and Ruth has been gleaning safely in Boaz's field, but nothing has changed in the women's future. They are two widows with no man to hold land or name for the family of Elimelech, and gleaning ends when harvest ends. Chapter 3 is where Naomi, who came home from Moab saying the LORD had emptied her, begins to act on hope. Her plan turns the question of chapter 2 (will Boaz be kind?) into a sharper one: will he take responsibility? The chapter ends with the matter nearly settled and one obstacle named, a nearer redeemer, which chapter 4 will resolve at the town gate.
historical:
The book sets its story in the days when the judges ruled (Ruth 1:1), the period before Israel had kings, usually placed in the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC. That was a violent and unstable time, as the book of Judges shows, and Ruth's quiet decency is a deliberate contrast. When the book itself was written is debated. Some scholars place it in the time of the monarchy, perhaps under David or Solomon, since it ends by tracing David's ancestry and treats the customs it describes as older than the reader's day (4:7). Others place it after the exile, in the Persian period, and read it partly as a gentle answer to the concern about foreign wives in Ezra and Nehemiah. The language and the customs are used as evidence on both sides, and no position commands agreement.

Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judah, sat in grain country; its name means house of bread. The barley harvest came in the spring, around April, and the wheat harvest a few weeks later, so this scene takes place late in the harvest season.
cultural:
Threshing and winnowing were done on a flat, hard open space, often a shared village floor on higher ground where the wind was reliable. After the stalks were beaten or trampled to loosen the grain, workers tossed the mixture into the air with forks, and the evening breeze carried off the chaff while the heavier grain fell back. The harvested grain was valuable and vulnerable, so owners and workers slept beside the heap to guard it. That is why Boaz is there at night, eating and drinking in the good spirits of a finished harvest.

Naomi's instructions have Ruth wash, anoint herself, and put on her cloak or best clothing, perhaps marking the end of her mourning as a widow. The central request uses a known gesture. To spread the corner of a garment over a woman was a way of taking her in marriage and under protection; Ezekiel 16:8 uses the same picture of God with Israel. Ruth also names Boaz as a go'el, a kinsman-redeemer. Under Israel's law the nearest male relative had duties to a family in trouble: to buy back land sold out of the family (Leviticus 25:25), to redeem a relative sold into debt slavery, and to avenge a killing. Marrying a dead man's widow to continue his name was a separate custom, levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10), which strictly applied to a brother. Ruth joins the two ideas, asking Boaz to redeem the family by marrying her, and Boaz treats the request as honorable rather than presumptuous.
literary: The chapter is built as a night scene framed by two conversations between Naomi and Ruth, one before (verses 1-5) and one after (verses 16-18). In the middle, the dialogue at the threshing floor is the turning point of the whole book. Much of the power lies in echoes of earlier chapters. In 2:12 Boaz prayed that Ruth would be rewarded by the LORD, under whose wings she had taken refuge; here Ruth asks him to spread the corner of his garment, the same Hebrew word, over her. In effect she asks Boaz to become the answer to his own prayer. In 2:1 Boaz was called a man of standing, and here he calls Ruth “a woman of noble character” (verse 11), using the same Hebrew word for worth; the two are matched. The ending also answers Naomi's bitter words in 1:21, where she said the LORD had brought her back empty. Now Boaz sends barley so that Ruth will not return “empty-handed” (verse 17), the same Hebrew word. The narrator keeps the scene discreet and suggestive, and the ambiguity is deliberate.

outline.t: Naomi's plan to find Ruth a home
Ruth at the threshing floor: the midnight request
Boaz's blessing, promise, and the nearer redeemer
Ruth leaves before dawn with six measures of barley
Naomi waits for Boaz to settle the matter

doctrines.note: God is never seen acting directly in this chapter, and no miracle occurs. Yet the reader has already been told that the LORD sees and rewards (2:12), and here his care works through a mother-in-law's plan, a woman's courage, and a man's integrity. Ruth teaches that God's providence often looks like ordinary people doing right at some risk.

The language of redemption is at the heart of the chapter. A redeemer is a relative who pays a cost to restore someone who cannot restore themselves. Israel's Scriptures also call God the Redeemer of his people, and Boaz's willingness gives that word a human face.

The chapter treats marriage as a matter of protection, provision, and continuing a family's name and land, not only of affection. Boaz honors Ruth's loyalty to Naomi and to her dead husband's family, and the whole plan is aimed at restoring a household that death had broken.

words.note: Ga'al, to redeem, and its participle go'el, redeemer. The verb means to act as the responsible kinsman: to buy back, restore, or take up a relative's cause. It appears seven times in this chapter alone. Elsewhere Isaiah repeatedly calls the LORD Israel's Redeemer, and in Ruth the family obligation becomes a picture of what God does.

Kanaph, a wing, and by extension the edge or corner of a garment. In 2:12 it is the LORD's wings under which Ruth took refuge; in 3:9 it is the corner of Boaz's garment. The repetition invites the reader to see Boaz's protection as the way God's protection reaches Ruth.

Hesed, often rendered kindness, loyalty, or steadfast love. It means faithful love that goes beyond what is strictly required, especially within a relationship of commitment. Boaz says Ruth's latest hesed is greater than her first: she has chosen to seek a redeemer who can carry on her husband's family rather than pursue a younger man for herself.

Manoach, a resting place. Naomi's opening question is literally whether she should seek rest for Ruth. The word points to settled security, a home and a husband, and recalls Naomi's prayer in 1:9 that her daughters-in-law would find rest in a husband's house.

christ: The link to Christ runs through two threads, one of lineage and one of pattern. By lineage, the marriage this chapter sets in motion produces Obed, the grandfather of David, and Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Boaz and Ruth among his ancestors (Matthew 1:5). A Moabite widow stands in the family line of the Messiah, which anticipates a gospel for the nations. By pattern, the kinsman-redeemer is a relative who takes on a cost to restore a family that cannot help itself. The New Testament speaks of Christ as the one who redeems his people at the cost of his own life and who shares our flesh and blood in order to do it (Hebrews 2:14). Ruth 3 does not predict Christ, and Boaz is not a coded figure. The connection is thematic: the Bible's language of redemption begins in ordinary family duty like this, and the gospel uses that language to describe what God has done in Jesus.

hard.q: What exactly happened at the threshing floor, and was Naomi's plan improper?
hard.a: The difficulty is real. Uncovering feet, lying down at night, and the verb to know all carry possible sexual overtones in Hebrew, and the word for feet can be a euphemism elsewhere. Some readers therefore think the scene involves at least the suggestion of seduction and that the narrator leaves it deliberately unclear. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, read it differently: Ruth's act is a bold but chaste proposal, the uncovering of Boaz's feet is a way of waking him and signaling her request without speaking in front of others, and the narrator's stress on Ruth's noble character, on Boaz's care for her reputation, and on his refusal to act until the nearer redeemer has been consulted shows that nothing improper took place. Both readings agree that the scene is charged and risky, that Ruth placed her reputation in Boaz's hands, and that Boaz responded with honor rather than advantage. The book's point is his integrity and her loyalty, not the details of the night.

questions: Boaz once prayed that God would shelter Ruth under his wings, and then became the means of that shelter. Where might you be the answer to a prayer you have prayed for someone else?
Ruth takes a real risk to ask for what she needs. What makes it hard to ask for help, and what does her example suggest about faith and initiative?
Boaz could have taken advantage of the situation, or simply claimed Ruth, but he honored the rights of the nearer relative. What does integrity look like when no one else would know?
